title: Felix Randal: occasion and date
short: An elegiac sonnet dated 28 April 1880 at Liverpool, for a parishioner identified as the farrier Felix Spencer, who died a week earlier.
body: Hopkins was a curate at the Jesuit church of St Francis Xavier in Liverpool from the end of 1879 to 1881, ministering in poor districts. Parish records studied by Alfred Thomas, S.J., identify the man behind the poem as Felix Spencer, a farrier who died, probably of pulmonary tuberculosis, on 21 April 1880; Hopkins had attended him in his illness. The manuscript is dated 28 April 1880. Hopkins altered the surname, perhaps for discretion; the new name also supplies the rhyme with 'sandal' that closes the poem, and Cotter suggests an echo of the ballad 'Lord Randal'. Like nearly all his mature poems it was unpublished in his lifetime, first appearing in Robert Bridges's edition of 1918. The Latin name Felix means 'happy' or 'fortunate', a resonance the poem's last lines seem to exploit.

title: farrier
short: A smith who makes and fits horseshoes, and often treats horses' ailments.
body: A farrier (Old French ferrier, from Latin ferrarius, 'of iron') is a blacksmith who specialises in shoeing horses; in the nineteenth century the trade also covered horse-doctoring. In industrial Liverpool, with its huge traffic of carts and dray horses, it was skilled and physically demanding work. The occupation gives the poem its controlling contrast: the powerful craftsman of iron, remembered in the last line, against the wasted invalid of the octave.

title: O he is dead then? my duty all ended
short: The priest receives the news of death; the tone has been read as cool and professional, as weary, or as tender understatement.
body: The poem begins in the middle of a conversation, as if the speaker has just been told of the death. 'My duty all ended' recalls that the priest's pastoral obligations to the dying man are now over. Readers differ on the tone: some find it detached, even brusque, a professional's acknowledgement of a case closed; others hear the shock and fatigue of a priest who had watched the man's long decline, and a self-reproach that the poem goes on to correct. The colloquial interjection 'O' and the questioning 'then?' mark it as speech, not formal elegy.

title: his mould of man, big-boned and hardy-handsome
short: 'Mould' means the frame or build of his body; the man was a powerful physical type, large-boned and robustly good-looking.
body: A 'mould' is a form or pattern from which something is cast, and so, by extension, a person's physical build. The phrase presents Felix as a fine specimen of a man, as if cast in a strong pattern. 'Hardy-handsome' is a characteristic Hopkins compound, fusing toughness and beauty. Some readers also hear 'mould' as earth or soil, anticipating the grave, though this sense is not certain. The archive text breaks the compound across a line ('hardy- / handsome'), reflecting the long lines of the manuscript.

title: Pining, pining, till time when reason rambled
short: He wasted away over a long illness until his mind wandered in delirium.
body: 'Pining' means wasting away through illness or suffering, and the repetition stretches out the long decline of tuberculosis (the length of Felix Spencer's illness is not firmly documented). 'Reason rambled' describes the delirium of the last stage: the mind wandered within the body ('in it', referring to the 'mould of man'). The alliteration of r and the internal rhyme 'rambled ... some' keep the sound dense even in a line of plain statement.

title: some / Fatal four disorders, fleshed there, all contended
short: Unspecified illnesses that fought over his body; the number four has prompted readings from medical complications to the four humours.
body: Hopkins does not name the 'four disorders'. The most literal reading takes them as several fatal illnesses or complications at once, such as tuberculosis with its attendant conditions. Others have proposed a symbolic sense: the four humours of older medicine, whose balance was thought to constitute health, or the four elements of which the body was composed. 'Fleshed there' means established, embedded in the flesh, and may also carry the hunting sense of 'to flesh' a hound, to give it a taste of blood. 'All contended' turns the body into a battlefield, preparing for the next line, 'Sickness broke him'.

title: Sickness broke him. Impatient he cursed at first
short: A blunt sentence after the long first quatrain; the strong man, at first rebellious, accepts his illness after receiving the sacraments.
body: The short declarative sentence is a deliberate contrast to the sprawling syntax of the first quatrain. 'Broke' fits both a body and a horse: the man who shod horses has himself been broken, as one breaks in a horse. Felix at first 'cursed' in impatience, then 'mended', not in health but in spirit, after receiving the last rites. The movement from rebellion to acceptance is the spiritual story the priest is able to tell, and it underlies the poem's final note of hope.

title: Being anointed and all
short: Felix received the sacrament of anointing of the sick (Extreme Unction); 'and all' is a colloquial shrug of Lancashire speech.
body: In Catholic practice the dying are anointed with holy oil by a priest, following James 5:14 ('Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord'). In Hopkins's time this was called Extreme Unction. The casual 'and all' imitates popular speech, as if the speaker were explaining matters to a parishioner, and it understates the sacrament's importance. The 'heavenlier heart' had begun even earlier, when he had first received Communion during his illness.

title: our sweet reprieve and ransom
short: Holy Communion, brought to him in illness: a 'reprieve' from spiritual death and the 'ransom' Christ paid for sinners.
body: The phrase is Hopkins's periphrasis for the Eucharist, which the priest 'tendered' (offered) to the sick man some months before his death. 'Reprieve' is a legal term for the suspension of a death sentence; 'ransom' echoes Christ's saying that the Son of Man came 'to give his life a ransom for many' (Matthew 20:28; Mark 10:45). 'Our' marks it as the shared possession of the faithful, priest and parishioner together. The alliteration and the warm adjective 'sweet' give the sacrament tenderness amid the poem's harder sounds.

title: God rest him all road ever he offended!
short: Lancashire dialect: 'all road' means 'in whatever way'; the priest prays for forgiveness of every way in which Felix may have sinned.
body: 'All road' (also 'all roads', 'any road') is a northern English dialect expression meaning 'in every way, however'. The prayer thus means 'God rest him, in whatever way he ever offended'. Hopkins took a keen interest in dialect and deliberately adopts the idiom of his Lancashire parishioners here, placing a popular phrase inside the ritual formula 'God rest him'. The effect is both affectionate and humble: the priest speaks the dead man's language.

title: This seeing the sick endears them to us
short: The sestet opens with a turn to reflection: ministering to the sick binds priest and patient; the chiasmus makes the endearment mutual.
body: Line 9 marks the volta of this Petrarchan sonnet (octave abbaabba, sestet ccdccd). The priest generalises: the act of visiting the sick makes them dear to us, and 'us too it endears' makes us dear to them, or makes us better. The inverted repetition (chiasmus) enacts reciprocity. The next line reverses the roles: 'My tongue had taught thee comfort, touch had quenched thy tears, / Thy tears that touched my heart'. The repetition of 'tears' and 'touch' ties the giver and receiver of comfort together. This answers the apparent coldness of 'my duty all ended'.

title: child, Felix, poor Felix Randal
short: The speaker turns from 'he' to 'thee', addressing the dead man directly; 'child' is a priest's word for a parishioner, ironic for this giant.
body: Until line 9 Felix is spoken of in the third person; from line 10 ('My tongue had taught thee comfort') the priest addresses him with the intimate 'thee' and 'thy', and line 11 names him. 'Child' expresses the spiritual fatherhood of the priest ('Father' Hopkins), and it is poignant because the big-boned farrier has become, in illness, as helpless as a child. The repeated name, with its gradual lengthening ('child, Felix, poor Felix Randal'), has the rhythm of lament.

anchor: How far from then forethought of
title: How far from then forethought of, all thy more boisterous years
short: In his vigorous years, no one then foresaw this end: the compressed syntax means 'how far from being foreseen at that time'.
body: The line is typically condensed. Paraphrased, it says: in all your more boisterous years, how far was this ending from being thought of beforehand. 'Forethought of' is a participle (foreseen) and 'then' refers to the time of his strength. 'Boisterous' suggests noisy, rough, high-spirited energy. The sestet moves back in time from deathbed to the forge, reversing the expected elegiac progression from life to death so that the poem ends on the man's power rather than his decline.

title: the random grim forge
short: 'Random' may mean built of irregular, unsquared stones (a mason's term), as well as haphazard or makeshift.
body: In building, 'random' describes masonry of stones of irregular size and shape, not laid in courses ('random rubble'); Hopkins, alert to technical vocabularies, probably intends this sense of a rough-built smithy. The more common sense, 'haphazard, untidy', is also present, and the word may echo 'Randal'. 'Grim' gives the smoky, dark forge a fierce character. The forge is where Felix was 'powerful amidst peers', the strong man among his fellow workers.

title: Didst fettle
short: Dialect: 'fettle' means to prepare, make ready, put in order; here, to make and fit a horseshoe.
body: 'Fettle' (from Middle English, of uncertain origin, related to an old word for a girdle) means to make ready, trim or put in good order, and survives in northern English dialect and in the phrase 'in fine fettle'. Here it describes the farrier forging and fitting a shoe. The archaic 'Didst' and 'thou' sit beside the dialect verb, a typical Hopkins mixture of the solemn and the vernacular.

title: the great grey drayhorse
short: A heavy, powerful horse used to draw a dray, a low cart for carrying heavy loads such as beer barrels.
body: A dray is a strong low cart without sides, used especially by brewers and for dock haulage; the large horses that pulled them were among the most familiar sights of Victorian Liverpool. The alliteration of 'great grey' and 'drayhorse' adds weight to the line. The horse's size and strength mirror Felix's own, and the final image puts the two great bodies together in the work of the forge.

title: his bright and battering sandal
short: The horseshoe, shining and made to pound the road, called a 'sandal'; the rhyme with 'Randal' is held back for the last word.
body: Calling a horseshoe a 'sandal' is surprising: it elevates the horse's iron shoe into something classical or even heroic, and its brightness suggests the light of the poem's close. 'Battering' looks forward to the shoe's work on the cobbled streets. The word supplies the delayed rhyme with 'Randal' (line 11), so that the sestet's c-rhyme closes on the man's name transformed into his craft. Many readers see in the bright final image a resurrection hint: the farrier, like the shoe he forged, is now made 'bright', or remembered in the radiance of his strength.

title: Sprung rhythm and the long sonnet line
short: A Petrarchan sonnet in Hopkins's sprung rhythm, with unusually long lines counted by stresses rather than syllables.
body: Hopkins's 'sprung rhythm', explained in the Author's Preface printed by Bridges in 1918, counts stresses, allowing a variable number of unstressed syllables between them. 'Felix Randal' uses long lines, often of six stresses, closer to the alexandrine than to the pentameter, which allows the colloquial, prose-like movement of the octave. The rhyme scheme is nevertheless strict Petrarchan (abbaabba ccdccd), with feminine and multi-syllable rhymes ('ended / contended', 'some / handsome', 'endears / tears'). The tension between the strict rhymes and the free, speaking rhythm is central to the poem's effect.
